label: thm:bounded-expansion
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:bounded-expansion}
Let $f_0\in\mathcal F$, with expansion
\begin{equation}\label{e3.7}
f_0(R\theta)=\sum_{k\geq1}\sum_{i=1}^{d_{k,N}}\alpha_k^iY_k^i(\theta).
\end{equation}
Then the solution of \eqref{e2.7} has the $L^2$ spherical harmonic expansion
\[
u_f'(r,\theta)=\sum_{k\geq1}\sum_{i=1}^{d_{k,N}}
(A_kr^k+B_kr^{2-N-k})\alpha_k^iY_k^i(\theta),
\]
where, for all $N\geq2$ and $k\geq1$,
\[
A_k=-\frac{Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}}{R^k-R^{2-N-k}},\qquad
B_k=\frac{Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}}{R^k-R^{2-N-k}}.
\]
head: environment

label: e3.8
title: Proof
body_md:
We first derive the equation satisfied by each spherical harmonic coefficient of the solution. Write $v=u_f'$ and, for $k\geq0$ and $1\leq i\leq d_{k,N}$, define
\[
v_k^i(r)=\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}v(r,\theta)Y_k^i(\theta)\,d\theta,
\qquad R\leq r\leq1.
\]
The solution $v$ belongs to $C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{A_0})$, so we can differentiate these coefficients twice with respect to $r$. In polar coordinates,
\[
\Delta v=\partial_{rr}v+\frac{N-1}{r}\partial_rv
+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}v.
\]
We multiply the equation $\Delta v=0$ by $Y_k^i$ and integrate over the sphere. Integration by parts on $\mathbb S^{N-1}$ gives
\[
\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\Delta_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}v\,Y_k^i\,d\theta
=\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}v\,\Delta_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}Y_k^i\,d\theta
=-k(k+N-2)v_k^i(r).
\]
Thus each coefficient satisfies
\[
(v_k^i)''+\frac{N-1}{r}(v_k^i)'
-\frac{k(k+N-2)}{r^2}v_k^i=0.
\]
The boundary conditions in \eqref{e2.7} imply
\[
v_k^i(1)=0,\qquad
v_k^i(R)=-Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}\alpha_k^i
\quad(k\geq1).
\]
The constant coefficient has zero data at both endpoints. Indeed,
\[
\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}f_0(R\theta)\,d\theta
=R^{1-N}\int_{\partial D_0}f_0=0.
\]
It follows that $v_0^1=0$. This explains why the expansion starts from $k=1$.

For $k\geq1$, we find the radial factor $S_k$ with inner value $-Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}$ and outer value zero. It solves
\begin{equation}\label{e3.8}
S_k''+\frac{N-1}{r}S_k'
-\frac{k(k+N-2)}{r^2}S_k=0,
\qquad R<r<1.
\end{equation}
Since this is an Euler equation, we substitute $S_k=r^a$. The characteristic equation is
\[
a(a-1)+(N-1)a-k(k+N-2)
=(a-k)(a+k+N-2)=0.
\]
Its roots are $k$ and $2-N-k$. They are distinct because $2k+N-2>0$. Therefore
\[
S_k(r)=A_kr^k+B_kr^{2-N-k}.
\]
The two boundary conditions give the linear system
\[
A_k+B_k=0,\qquad
A_kR^k+B_kR^{2-N-k}=-Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}.
\]
We first obtain $B_k=-A_k$ from the outer condition. Substitution into the inner condition yields
\[
A_k=-\frac{Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}}{R^k-R^{2-N-k}},\qquad
B_k=\frac{Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}}{R^k-R^{2-N-k}}.
\]
The denominator is nonzero: with $m_k=2k+N-2>0$,
\[
R^k-R^{2-N-k}=R^{2-N-k}(R^{m_k}-1)<0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
S_k(r)=-Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}
\frac{r^k-r^{2-N-k}}{R^k-R^{2-N-k}}.
\]
This formula also applies when $N=2$ and $k\geq1$: the two radial powers are $r^k$ and $r^{-k}$. The repeated-root case, with radial solutions $1$ and $\log r$, occurs only when $N=2$ and $k=0$, whose coefficient has already been shown to vanish.

Uniqueness for the radial boundary value problem now gives $v_k^i=\alpha_k^iS_k$. For each fixed $r\in[R,1]$, completeness of the spherical harmonics reconstructs $v(r,\cdot)$ in $L^2(\mathbb S^{N-1})$ and proves the stated expansion. The same projection calculation applied to the radial derivative gives
\[
(v_k^i)'(r)=\alpha_k^iA_k
\big(k r^{k-1}+(N+k-2)r^{1-N-k}\big).
\]
In particular, because the fluid normal on the inner sphere is $\mathbf n=-\partial_r$, the coefficients of its Neumann trace are
\[
\int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\partial_{\mathbf n}v(R,\theta)
Y_k^i(\theta)\,d\theta
=-\alpha_k^iA_k
\big(kR^{k-1}+(N+k-2)R^{1-N-k}\big).
\]
These are the coefficients used in the linearized boundary operator below.
head: environment

label: e3.12
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be the inner Dirichlet-to-Neumann map for harmonic functions on $A_0$ with zero outer Dirichlet data, acting from $C^{2,\alpha}(\partial D_0)$ to $C^{1,\alpha}(\partial D_0)$. This map is an isomorphism: for any inner Neumann datum $h\in C^{1,\alpha}$, the mixed problem
\begin{equation}\label{e3.12}
\left\{
\begin{array}{ll}
-\Delta w=0 &\text{in }A_0,\\
w=0 &\text{on }\partial\Omega_0,\\
\partial_{\mathbf n}w=h &\text{on }\partial D_0
\end{array}
\right.
\end{equation}
has a unique $C^{2,\alpha}$ solution and a Schauder estimate, since the two boundary components are disjoint and the outer Dirichlet condition removes the constant ambiguity \cite{Gilbarg}. Its inner trace is $T^{-1}h$.

Moreover $T:\mathcal F\to\mathcal H$ is also an isomorphism. Spherical averaging shows that mean-zero inner Dirichlet data give mean-zero inner Neumann data. Conversely, if $h$ has zero mean in \eqref{e3.12}, the spherical average of $w$ has zero outer value and zero inner normal derivative, and is identically zero; thus its inner trace has zero mean.

By \eqref{e2.7} and \eqref{e3.2},
\[
\partial_f\Psi(0,0)=-Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}T+\kappa_R^{\mathrm{bd}}J,
\]
where $J:\mathcal F\to\mathcal H$ is the compact inclusion $C^{2,\alpha}\hookrightarrow C^{1,\alpha}$. The operator is therefore Fredholm of index zero. Formula \eqref{e3.10} shows that its kernel is zero, so it is an isomorphism. This argument establishes the H\"older inverse directly; nonzero multipliers alone would not justify an inverse between these spaces.

The implicit function theorem now gives a unique smooth map $g\mapsto f(g)\in\mathcal F$ solving \eqref{e3.1}, with $f(0)=0$. The resulting constant is
\[
Q(g)=\frac1{|\partial D_0|}\int_{\partial D_0}q_{f(g),g}.
\]
It is positive for small $g$ by continuity from $Q_R^{\mathrm{bd}}>0$. This proves the theorem.

label: thm3.1
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Work on the compact quotient $A_R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$. Uniform ellipticity and the Dirichlet Schauder estimates give existence and uniqueness. The coefficients depend smoothly on $\phi$, so the inverse Dirichlet operator and the solution map are smooth. Rotations in $x$ and reflection in $t$ preserve the equation and the boundary data, and uniqueness gives the asserted symmetries. Solving the radial Poisson equation gives \eqref{eq3.6}. This is the same fixed-domain method used for periodic overdetermined problems in \cite{FallMW}.
head: environment

label: lem3.2
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
At the physical point $(\phi(t)e_1,t)$, the gradient of the radial profile is $(U_R'(\phi(t))e_1,0)$. By \eqref{eq3.4} and \eqref{eq3.5},
\[
\partial_{\nu_\phi}u^\phi(Re_1,t)
=-\frac{U_R'(\phi(t))}{\sqrt{1+\phi'(t)^2}}.
\]
This expression is smooth from a neighborhood of $R$ in $X$ to $Y$. Along $\phi_\varepsilon=R+\varepsilon\psi$, the physical normal is
\[
\mathbf n_{\phi_\varepsilon}(\phi_\varepsilon(t)e_1,t)
=\frac{(-e_1,\varepsilon\psi'(t))}{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2\psi'(t)^2}}
=(-e_1,0)+\varepsilon(0,\psi'(t))+O(\varepsilon^2).
\]
The remainder is taken in $C^{1,\alpha}$ as a function of $t$. Its first variation is tangential to the reference cylinder, so it has zero scalar product with the reference radial gradient. Equivalently,
\[
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
\big(1+\varepsilon^2\psi'(t)^2\big)^{-1/2}=0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
\partial_{\nu_{\phi_\varepsilon}}u^{\phi_\varepsilon}(Re_1,t)
&=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
\left[-U_R'(R+\varepsilon\psi(t))
\big(1+\varepsilon^2\psi'(t)^2\big)^{-1/2}\right]\\
&=-U_R''(R)\psi(t)
=-\kappa_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}\psi(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves \eqref{eq3.11}, including the case $n=2$.
head: environment

label: thm3.3
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq3.21
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $a_\phi=u^\phi-u_\phi$. Subtracting the two equations \eqref{eq3.10} and \eqref{eq3.2} cancels their common constant right-hand side. The boundary values described above therefore give
\begin{equation}\label{eq3.21}
-\Delta_{g_\phi}a_\phi=0,\qquad
a_\phi=U_R(\phi(t))-1\ \text{on }|x|=R,\qquad
a_\phi=0\ \text{on }|x|=1.
\end{equation}
At $\phi\equiv R$, both $u^R$ and $u_R$ equal $U_R(|x|)$, so $a_R=0$ throughout $A_R$.

The smooth dependence in Theorem~\ref{thm3.1} allows us to differentiate $a_\phi$ in $C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{A_R})$. Define its material derivative by
\[
b_{\psi,R}=D_\phi a_\phi\big|_{\phi=R}[\psi]
=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}a_{\phi_\varepsilon}.
\]
This derivative is taken with the reference point $(x,t)$ fixed. In general it differs from the Eulerian derivative of the physical function by the transport term. Indeed, if $\widehat a_\phi=U_R-\widehat u_\phi$ and $a'_{\psi,R}$ denotes its derivative at a fixed interior physical point, then
\[
b_{\psi,R}=a'_{\psi,R}
+\nabla\widehat a_R\cdot\mathbf p_\psi.
\]
Here $\widehat a_R=0$, so the transport term vanishes and the two derivatives agree.

To differentiate the equation, put $\mathcal A_\varepsilon=-\Delta_{g_\varepsilon}$. These operators depend smoothly on $\varepsilon$ as bounded maps from $C^{2,\alpha}$ to $C^{0,\alpha}$ on the fixed quotient. Differentiating $\mathcal A_\varepsilon a_{\phi_\varepsilon}=0$ gives
\[
\mathcal A_0b_{\psi,R}
+\left.\frac{d\mathcal A_\varepsilon}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}a_R=0.
\]
The second term is zero because $a_R$ is identically zero. Thus no variation of the coefficients contributes to the equation for $b_{\psi,R}$. By \eqref{eq3.1}, this equation is
\[
\Delta_xb_{\psi,R}+\partial_{tt}b_{\psi,R}=0\qquad\text{in }A_R.
\]
On the fixed inner boundary, differentiation of \eqref{eq3.21} yields
\[
b_{\psi,R}(R\theta,t)
=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
\big(U_R(R+\varepsilon\psi(t))-1\big)
=U_R'(R)\psi(t)=-Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}\psi(t).
\]
The outer boundary value in \eqref{eq3.21} is zero for every $\varepsilon$, so $b_{\psi,R}=0$ on $|x|=1$. Comparison with \eqref{eq3.20} and uniqueness of the Dirichlet problem give
\[
b_{\psi,R}=-Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}w_{\psi,R}.
\]

It remains to differentiate the normal trace of $a_\phi$. A metric normal derivative can be written as $\partial_{\nu_\phi}a_\phi=da_\phi(\nu_\phi)$. Hence, at a fixed point of $|x|=R$,
\[
\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
\big(da_{\phi_\varepsilon}(\nu_{\phi_\varepsilon})\big)
=db_{\psi,R}(\nu)
+da_R\left(\left.\frac{d\nu_{\phi_\varepsilon}}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}\right).
\]
The second term, which contains the variation of the pulled-back unit normal, vanishes because $da_R=0$. The variation of the metric is already included in the variation of $\nu_\phi$ in this directional-derivative formula. We obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq3.24}
D_\phi\big|_{\phi=R}\big(\partial_{\nu_\phi}a_\phi\big)[\psi]
=\partial_\nu b_{\psi,R}.
\end{equation}

Since $u_\phi=u^\phi-a_\phi$, Lemma~\ref{lem3.2} and \eqref{eq3.24}, evaluated at $(Re_1,t)$, now give
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_R\psi
&=-\kappa_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}\psi
-\partial_\nu b_{\psi,R}(Re_1,\cdot)\\
&=Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}\partial_\nu w_{\psi,R}(Re_1,\cdot)
-\kappa_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}\psi.
\end{aligned}
\]
The parameter $R$ is held fixed in $D_\varphi H(R,0)$, so the term $Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}$ subtracted in \eqref{eq3.7} has no variation here. This proves \eqref{eq3.19}. Equivalently, if
\[
T_R\psi=\partial_\nu w_{\psi,R}(Re_1,\cdot),
\]
then $L_R=Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}T_R-\kappa_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}J$, where $J:X\hookrightarrow Y$ is the natural inclusion.

label: thm3.4
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: lem:cyl-modes
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cyl-modes}
For every $R\in(0,1)$ and $0\leq k<\ell$, $\mu_\ell(R)>\mu_k(R)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We compare the normalized solutions $p_k$ and $p_\ell$ at the same radius $R$. The maximum principle gives $0<p_j<1$ on $(R,1)$ for $j=k,\ell$, including $j=0$. In divergence form, their equations are
\[
(r^{n-1}p_j')'=j^2r^{n-1}p_j.
\]
Multiplying the equation for $p_\ell$ by $p_k$, multiplying the equation for $p_k$ by $p_\ell$, and subtracting, we obtain
\[
\frac{d}{dr}\left[r^{n-1}(p_\ell'p_k-p_k'p_\ell)\right]
=(\ell^2-k^2)r^{n-1}p_kp_\ell.
\]
At $r=1$, the expression in brackets vanishes because both functions are zero. At $r=R$, both are $1$, so this expression equals $R^{n-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)$. Integration from $R$ to $1$ therefore yields
\[
R^{n-1}\big(\mu_\ell(R)-\mu_k(R)\big)
=(\ell^2-k^2)\int_R^1r^{n-1}p_kp_\ell\,dr>0.
\]
This proves the strict comparison for every pair of modes, including the constant mode.
head: environment

label: lem:cyl-radius
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cyl-radius}
For each $k\geq1$, $M_k(R):=R\mu_k(R)$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$, and
\[
\lim_{R\to0^+}M_k(R)=n-2,\qquad
\lim_{R\to1^-}M_k(R)=+\infty.
\]
The first limit equals zero when $n=2$.
head: environment

label: eq:cyl-riccati
title: Proof
body_md:
We fix $k\geq1$. The function $Z_k$ in \eqref{eq:cyl-bessel} is independent of the inner radius $R$, so
\[
\mu_k(R)=-\frac{Z_k'(R)}{Z_k(R)}.
\]
We already know that $Z_k>0$ and $Z_k'<0$ on $(0,1)$. The derivative sign can also be seen directly from its equation:
\[
(r^{n-1}Z_k')'=k^2r^{n-1}Z_k>0,\qquad
r^{n-1}Z_k'(r)
=-1-k^2\int_r^1s^{n-1}Z_k(s)\,ds<0.
\]
We set
\[
y(r)=-\frac{rZ_k'(r)}{Z_k(r)}>0,
\qquad M_k(R)=y(R).
\]
Differentiating this quotient and using $Z_k''=k^2Z_k-(n-1)Z_k'/r$, we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
ry'
&=-\frac{rZ_k'}{Z_k}-\frac{r^2Z_k''}{Z_k}
+r^2\left(\frac{Z_k'}{Z_k}\right)^2\\
&=y+(n-1)\frac{rZ_k'}{Z_k}-k^2r^2+y^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $y$ satisfies the Riccati equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cyl-riccati}
ry'=y^2-(n-2)y-k^2r^2.
\end{equation}
The positive root of the polynomial on the right is
\[
c(r)=\frac{n-2+\sqrt{(n-2)^2+4k^2r^2}}2,
\qquad
c'(r)=\frac{2k^2r}{\sqrt{(n-2)^2+4k^2r^2}}>0.
\]
The other root is negative for $r>0$. Hence, because $y>0$, the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:cyl-riccati} is positive exactly when $y>c$. For $n=2$ we have $c(r)=kr$ and $c'(r)=k>0$.

We next prove that $y(r)>c(r)$ for all $0<r<1$. Since $Z_k(1)=0$ and $Z_k'(1)=-1$, Taylor expansion at $1$ gives
\[
Z_k(r)=(1-r)+O((1-r)^2),\qquad
Z_k'(r)=-1+O(1-r).
\]
It follows that $y(r)\to+\infty$ as $r\to1^-$, whereas $c(r)$ remains bounded there. Thus $y-c>0$ on a neighborhood of $1$. If the assertion fails, choose $a\in(0,1)$ with $y(a)-c(a)\leq0$ and then $b\in(a,1)$ such that $y-c>0$ on $[b,1)$. Continuity gives a nonempty closed set of contact points in $[a,b]$. Let $r_0$ be its largest point. There are no contact points to its right, and the positivity near $1$ gives $y-c>0$ on $(r_0,1)$. Therefore
\[
(y-c)'(r_0)\geq0.
\]
But $y(r_0)=c(r_0)$ makes the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:cyl-riccati} zero, so $y'(r_0)=0$ and
\[
(y-c)'(r_0)=-c'(r_0)<0,
\]
a contradiction. We conclude that $y>c$ and hence $y'>0$ on $(0,1)$. This proves the strict increase of $M_k$.

We now check its limit at zero. When $n>2$, we have $\beta>0$, and the small-argument forms in \cite[Section 10.30]{DLMF} are
\[
I_\beta(s)\sim\frac{s^\beta}{2^\beta\Gamma(\beta+1)},
\qquad
K_\beta(s)\sim2^{\beta-1}\Gamma(\beta)s^{-\beta}.
\]
In \eqref{eq:cyl-bessel}, the $K_\beta(kr)$ term is the leading term. Thus
\[
Z_k(r)\sim C_k r^{-2\beta}=C_k r^{2-n},
\qquad
C_k=2^{\beta-1}\Gamma(\beta)k^{-\beta}I_\beta(k)>0.
\]
To obtain the derivative asymptotic, we use the exact derivative formula above, together with
\[
K_{\beta+1}(s)\sim2^\beta\Gamma(\beta+1)s^{-\beta-1},
\qquad
I_{\beta+1}(s)\sim\frac{s^{\beta+1}}{2^{\beta+1}\Gamma(\beta+2)}.
\]
This gives
\[
Z_k'(r)\sim-2\beta C_k r^{-2\beta-1}
=-(n-2)C_k r^{1-n},
\qquad
-\frac{rZ_k'(r)}{Z_k(r)}\longrightarrow n-2.
\]
In this step, the derivative asymptotic follows from the Bessel derivative identities, rather than from differentiating an asymptotic equivalence.

For $n=2$, we have $\beta=0$. The corresponding forms are
\[
I_0(s)\sim1,\qquad K_0(s)\sim\log(1/s),
\qquad I_1(s)\sim\frac{s}{2},\qquad K_1(s)\sim\frac1s.
\]
Using \eqref{eq:cyl-bessel} and its derivative formula with $\beta=0$, we obtain
\[
Z_k(r)\sim I_0(k)\log(1/r),\qquad
Z_k'(r)\sim-\frac{I_0(k)}r,
\qquad
-\frac{rZ_k'(r)}{Z_k(r)}\sim\frac1{\log(1/r)}\longrightarrow0.
\]
This establishes the zero-end limit also in dimension $n=2$. Finally, the Taylor expansion at $1$ gives $y(r)\sim r/(1-r)$, so the other limit is $+\infty$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first take $\gamma=0$. Then $U_R=p_0(\cdot;R)$, so $Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}=\mu_0(R)>0$, and
\[
\frac{\kappa_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}}{Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}}
=\frac{n-1}{R},\qquad
\Lambda_1(R,0)=\frac{Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}}{R}\big(M_1(R)-(n-1)\big).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:cyl-radius}, $M_1$ increases strictly from $n-2$ to $+\infty$. Since $n-2<n-1$, there is exactly one $R_0\in(0,1)$ with $M_1(R_0)=n-1$. Substitution of this value into \eqref{eq:cyl-riccati}, with $k=1$, gives
\[
M_1'(R_0)
=\frac{(n-1)^2-(n-2)(n-1)-R_0^2}{R_0}
=\frac{n-1-R_0^2}{R_0}>0.
\]
The last inequality follows from $n\geq2$ and $R_0<1$; in particular, it is strict when $n=2$. When we differentiate the formula for $\Lambda_1(R,0)$, the derivative of $Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}/R$ is multiplied by $M_1(R)-(n-1)$ and therefore contributes zero at the root. Consequently,
\[
\partial_R\Lambda_1(R_0,0)
=\frac{Q_{R_0}^{\mathrm{cyl}}}{R_0}M_1'(R_0)>0.
\]

The Bessel quotient is smooth for $0<R<1$, and the formulas in \eqref{eq3.6} show that $Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}$ and $\kappa_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}$ are smooth in $(R,\gamma)$. Thus $(R,\gamma)\mapsto\Lambda_1(R,\gamma)$ is smooth near $(R_0,0)$. The implicit function theorem gives a smooth root $R_*=R_*(n,\gamma)$ near $R_0$ for sufficiently small $|\gamma|$. We shrink $\gamma_{\mathrm{cyl}}(n)>0$ so that $R_*\in(0,1)$, $Q_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}>0$, and $\partial_R\Lambda_1(R_*,\gamma)>0$ throughout this interval.

At the root, the equation $\Lambda_1(R_*,\gamma)=0$ is exactly $\kappa_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}=Q_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}\mu_1(R_*)$. Hence for every $k\geq0$,
\[
\Lambda_k(R_*,\gamma)
=Q_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}\big(\mu_k(R_*)-\mu_1(R_*)\big).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:cyl-modes} gives $\mu_0<\mu_1$ and $\mu_k>\mu_1$ for every $k\geq2$. Since $Q_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}>0$, these inequalities prove the stated signs, including the negative constant multiplier. This exact comparison establishes nonresonance for all modes at once, with the same interval of allowed $\gamma$.
head: environment

label: lem:cyl-fredholm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cyl-fredholm}
At $R_*$, $L_{R_*}:X\to Y$ is Fredholm of index zero, with
\[
\ker L_{R_*}=\operatorname{span}\{\cos t\},\qquad
\operatorname{Range}L_{R_*}
=\left\{h\in Y:\int_0^{2\pi}h(t)\cos t\,dt=0\right\}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
D_R D_\varphi H(R_*,0)[\cos t]
\notin\operatorname{Range}L_{R_*}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We write $T_R:X\to Y$ for the inner Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator in \eqref{eq3.20}, namely $T_R\psi=\partial_\nu w_{\psi,R}(Re_1,\cdot)$. The Dirichlet Schauder estimate and the boundary trace estimate make $T_R$ bounded. We first show that it is an isomorphism. On the compact quotient $A_R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$, consider
\[
\Delta w=0,\qquad w=0\ \text{on }|x|=1,\qquad
\partial_\nu w=h(t)\ \text{on }|x|=R.
\]
The outer Dirichlet condition removes the constant ambiguity and gives a coercive mixed boundary problem. Its two boundary components are disjoint and smooth, so the mixed boundary Schauder estimates yield a unique solution with
\[
\|w\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}\leq C_R\|h\|_{C^{1,\alpha}}
\quad(h\in Y);
\]
see \cite{Gilbarg}. Uniqueness makes this solution radial in $x$ and even in $t$. Its inner trace $\psi(t)=w(Re_1,t)$ belongs to $X$ and satisfies $T_R\psi=h$, with a bounded trace estimate. For injectivity, if $T_R\psi=0$, Green's identity for its harmonic extension gives $\int|\nabla w_{\psi,R}|^2=0$. The extension is constant and vanishes on the outer boundary, so it is zero and $\psi=0$. This proves that $T_R^{-1}:Y\to X$ is bounded.

By \eqref{eq3.19},
\[
L_R=Q_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}T_R-\kappa_R^{\mathrm{cyl}}J,
\]
where the inclusion $J:X\hookrightarrow Y$ is compact. At $R_*$, the scalar $Q_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}$ is positive, so $Q_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}T_{R_*}$ is an isomorphism. Equivalently,
\[
L_{R_*}=Q_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}T_{R_*}
\left(I-\frac{\kappa_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}}{Q_{R_*}^{\mathrm{cyl}}}
T_{R_*}^{-1}J\right).
\]
The operator in parentheses is the identity minus a compact operator on $X$. Therefore $L_{R_*}$ is Fredholm of index zero and its range is closed.

The cosine projection identities established above show that $L_{R_*}\psi=0$ forces
\[
\Lambda_k(R_*,\gamma)\widehat\psi_k=0
\quad\text{for every }k\geq0.
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm3.4}, only $k=1$ has zero multiplier. Thus every coefficient other than $\widehat\psi_1$ vanishes. Completeness in $L^2$ gives $\psi=\widehat\psi_1\cos t$, and continuity gives the same identity pointwise. Conversely, $L_{R_*}\cos t=0$. Hence the kernel is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\cos t\}$, and the index-zero property gives a range of codimension one.

To identify this range, we use Green's identity. For $\psi,\zeta\in X$, let $w_\psi$ and $w_\zeta$ be their harmonic extensions with zero outer boundary values. On the compact quotient,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{A_R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)}\nabla w_\psi\cdot\nabla w_\zeta
&=\int_{\partial(A_R/(2\pi\mathbb Z))}w_\zeta\partial_\nu w_\psi\\
&=|\mathbb S^{n-1}|R^{n-1}
\int_0^{2\pi}\zeta(t)(T_R\psi)(t)\,dt.
\end{aligned}
\]
The outer boundary term vanishes. Interchanging $\psi$ and $\zeta$ leaves the volume integral unchanged; cancelling the common inner surface factor gives
\[
\int_0^{2\pi}(T_R\psi)\zeta\,dt
=\int_0^{2\pi}\psi(T_R\zeta)\,dt.
\]
The scalar multiplication term in $L_R$ has the same symmetry. Therefore $L_{R_*}\cos t=0$ implies
\[
\int_0^{2\pi}(L_{R_*}\psi)(t)\cos t\,dt=0
\quad\text{for every }\psi\in X.
\]
The hyperplane defined by this integral has codimension one in $Y$. Since the closed range of $L_{R_*}$ also has codimension one and is contained in that hyperplane, the two spaces coincide.

Finally, the Banach spaces $X$ and $Y$ use the same periodic variable for all $R$, and $H$ depends smoothly on $R$. We can differentiate the identity $L_R\cos t=\Lambda_1(R,\gamma)\cos t$ with respect to $R$, keeping $\gamma$ fixed. This gives
\[
D_R D_\varphi H(R_*,0)[\cos t]
=\partial_R\Lambda_1(R_*,\gamma)\cos t.
\]
Its pairing with $\cos t$ is
\[
\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_R\Lambda_1(R_*,\gamma)\cos^2t\,dt
=\pi\partial_R\Lambda_1(R_*,\gamma)\ne0.
\]
It therefore lies outside the range just identified. This proves transversality.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $|\gamma|<\gamma_{\mathrm{cyl}}(n)$. Choose an open neighborhood $\mathcal U\subset(0,1)\times X$ of $(R_*,0)$ small enough that $0<R+\varphi(t)<1$ for every $(R,\varphi)\in\mathcal U$ and that the fixed-domain construction applies. The map $H:\mathcal U\to Y$ is smooth, and $H(R,0)=0$ for all $R$ sufficiently close to $R_*$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cyl-fredholm}, its derivative in $\varphi$ has a one-dimensional kernel, a codimension-one range, and satisfies the transversality condition. The Crandall--Rabinowitz theorem \cite[Theorem 1.7]{Crandall} gives a smooth curve $(R_s,\varphi_s)$ of zeros with
\[
R_0=R_*,\qquad
\varphi_s=s\cos t+s\mu_s,\qquad
\mu_0=0,\qquad
\int_0^{2\pi}\mu_s(t)\cos t\,dt=0.
\]
Here we use the closed complement of $\operatorname{span}\{\cos t\}$ defined by this integral condition. Smoothness of the curve follows from smoothness of $H$ and the implicit function theorem in the usual simple-eigenvalue reduction.

After reducing $\varepsilon$, $0<R_s+\varphi_s<1$ and $Q_{R_s}^{\mathrm{cyl}}>0$. Returning from the fixed quotient to the physical periodic domain yields the solution of \eqref{e1.6}. For $s\ne0$,
\[
\int_0^{2\pi}\phi_s(t)\cos t\,dt=\pi s\ne0,
\]
so the inner radius is nonconstant. This proves the claimed nontriviality and completes the theorem.
